p: You'll know you've arrived when you see the huge fin whale skeleton hanging beneath a glass canopy at the entrance. It's an incredible welcome, and it's worth standing underneath and just looking up for a minute before you go in. The museum reopened in 2018 after a major redevelopment, so the galleries feel bright and modern.

This museum's collections have serious scientific pedigree. Among them are specimens collected by Charles Darwin, who studied at Cambridge, including some from his voyage on HMS Beagle. Darwin was an obsessive beetle collector as a student, so look out for the insects. There's also a dodo skeleton, one of the rare examples of this famously extinct bird, which always draws a crowd. Kids love trying to imagine what it looked like with feathers on.

Entry is free, and allow around one to two hours, depending on how much your group loves animals. It's a great choice for a short, focused visit, and you can easily pop in more than once during a longer stay.

The museum sits on the Downing Site, and its neighbours are well worth adding on. The Sedgwick Museum of Earth Sciences is packed with fossils, rocks and dinosaurs, while the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology is just across the street with objects from around the world. Both are free too, making this little corner of Cambridge a brilliant spot for a rainy day. When you're done, the colleges and the river are only a short stroll away.
